claim: Neurons in multiple sensory areas respond more strongly to novel in comparison to familiar stimuli.
source: Neurons in multiple sensory areas respond more strongly to novel in comparison to familiar stimuli.
evidence: This is a general statement about experimental observations in neuroscience, presented as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Spike-timing-dependent plasticity of inhibitory-to-excitatory synapses generates novelty responses in a recurrent spiking network model.
source: Here, we show that spike-timing-dependent plasticity of inhibitory-to-excitatory synapses generates novelty responses in a recurrent spiking network model.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by computational modeling results shown throughout the manuscript.

claim: Inhibitory plasticity increases the inhibition onto excitatory neurons tuned to familiar stimuli, while inhibition for novel stimuli remains low, leading to a network novelty response.
source: Inhibitory plasticity increases the inhibition onto excitatory neurons tuned to familiar stimuli, while inhibition for novel stimuli remains low, leading to a network novelty response.
evidence: This mechanism is demonstrated through the model simulations and weight dynamics shown in Figure 4.

claim: The generation of novelty responses does not depend on the periodicity but rather on the distribution of presented stimuli.
source: The generation of novelty responses does not depend on the periodicity but rather on the distribution of presented stimuli.
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3E where shuffling stimuli within a sequence still generates novelty responses.

claim: By including tuning of inhibitory neurons, the network further captures stimulus-specific adaptation.
source: By including tuning of inhibitory neurons, the network further captures stimulus-specific adaptation.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6 where the model with tuned inhibitory neurons shows stimulus-specific adaptation.

claim: Disinhibition can control the amplification of novelty responses.
source: Finally, we suggest that disinhibition can control the amplification of novelty responses.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7 where disinhibition increases the amplitude and density of novelty responses.

claim: Local neural circuits perform computations on incoming sensory stimuli in an efficient manner by maximizing transmitted information or minimizing metabolic cost.
source: Local neural circuits perform computations on incoming sensory stimuli in an efficient manner by maximizing transmitted information or minimizing metabolic cost (Simoncelli and Olshausen, 2001; Barlow, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous theoretical work on efficient coding.

claim: Repeated or predictable stimuli do not provide new meaningful information.
source: Repeated or predictable stimuli do not provide new meaningful information.
evidence: This is a theoretical principle from predictive coding framework.

claim: Responses to repeated stimuli are suppressed according to the framework of predictive coding.
source: As a consequence, one should expect that responses to repeated stimuli are suppressed – a phenomenon postulated by the framework of predictive coding (Clark, 2013; Spratling, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to predictive coding literature.

claim: Sensory circuits across different modalities can encode a sequence or expectation violation and can detect novelty.
source: Recent experiments have demonstrated that sensory circuits across different modalities can encode a sequence or expectation violation and can detect novelty (Keller et al., 2012; Natan et al., 2015; Zmarz and Keller, 2016; Hamm and Yuste, 2016; Homann et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple experimental citations.

claim: Adaptation can occur over a wide range of timescales, which range from milliseconds to seconds.
source: Adaptation can occur over a wide range of timescales, which range from milliseconds to seconds (Ulanovsky et al., 2004; Lundstrom et al., 2010), and to multiple days in the case of behavioral habituation (Haak et al., 2014; Ramaswami, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The mismatch negativity (MMN) is classically detected in electroencephalography (EEG) data and often based on an auditory or visual 'oddball' paradigm.
source: At the scale of whole brain regions, a widely studied phenomenon is the mismatch negativity (MMN), which is classically detected in electroencephalography (EEG) data and often based on an auditory or visual 'oddball' paradigm (Näätänen et al., 1982; Hamm and Yuste, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental literature on MMN.

claim: Stimulus-specific adaptation (SSA) has been observed in multiple brain areas, most commonly reported in the primary auditory cortex.
source: SSA has been observed in multiple brain areas, most commonly reported in the primary auditory cortex (Ulanovsky et al., 2003; Yaron et al., 2012; Natan et al., 2015; Seay et al., 2020) and the primary visual cortex (Movshon and Lennie, 1979; Hamm and Yuste, 2016; Vinken et al., 2017; Homann et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple experimental citations.

claim: SSA has been found at different earlier stages including the retina and the visual thalamic nuclei.
source: Along the visual pathway, SSA has also been found at different earlier stages including the retina (Schwartz et al., 2007; Geffen et al., 2007; Schwartz and Berry, 2008) and the visual thalamic nuclei (Dhruv and Carandini, 2014; King et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Most models of SSA in primary sensory areas of the cortex focus on short-term plasticity and the depression of thalamocortical feedforward synapses.
source: Most models of SSA in primary sensory areas of the cortex focus on short-term plasticity and the depression of thalamocortical feedforward synapses (Mill et al., 2011a; Mill et al., 2011b; Park and Geffen, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous modeling studies.

claim: Recent experimental studies suggest that inhibition and the plasticity of inhibitory synapses shape the responses to repeated and novel stimuli.
source: Recent experimental studies suggest that inhibition and the plasticity of inhibitory synapses shape the responses to repeated and novel stimuli (Chen et al., 2015; Kato et al., 2015; Natan et al., 2015; Hamm and Yuste, 2016; Natan et al., 2017; Heintz et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent experimental work.

claim: In the mouse auditory cortex, both parvalbumin-positive (PV) and somatostatin-positive (SOM) interneurons contribute to SSA.
source: Natan and colleagues observed that in the mouse auditory cortex, both parvalbumin-positive (PV) and somatostatin-positive (SOM) interneurons contribute to SSA (Natan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Natan et al., 2015.

claim: Neurons that are more strongly adapted receive stronger inhibitory input than less adapted neurons, suggesting potentiation of inhibitory synapses as an underlying mechanism.
source: Furthermore, neurons that are more strongly adapted receive stronger inhibitory input than less adapted neurons, suggesting potentiation of inhibitory synapses as an underlying mechanism (Natan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Natan et al., 2017.

claim: Habituated behavior in Drosophila results from prolonged activation of an odor-specific excitatory subnetwork, which leads to the selective strengthening of inhibitory synapses onto the excitatory subnetwork.
source: Habituated behavior in Drosophila, for example, results from prolonged activation of an odor-specific excitatory subnetwork, which leads to the selective strengthening of inhibitory synapses onto the excitatory subnetwork (Das et al., 2011; Glanzman, 2011; Ramaswami, 2014; Barron et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental work in Drosophila.

claim: The model network is based on a recurrent spiking neural network model of the mammalian cortex with biologically inspired plasticity mechanisms.
source: We base our study on a recurrent spiking neural network model of the mammalian cortex with biologically inspired plasticity mechanisms that can generate assemblies in connectivity and attractors in activity to represent the stimulus-specific activation of specific sub-circuits (Litwin-Kumar and Doiron, 2014; Zenke et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the model architecture used in the study, supported by citations to previous modeling work.

claim: The model includes stimulus-specific input not only to the excitatory but also to the inhibitory population, as found experimentally.
source: We model excitatory and inhibitory neurons and include stimulus-specific input not only to the excitatory but also to the inhibitory population, as found experimentally (Ma et al., 2010; Griffen and Maffei, 2014; Znamenskiy et al., 2018).
evidence: This modeling choice is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Tuned inhibition leads to the formation of specific inhibitory-to-excitatory connections through inhibitory plasticity.
source: This additional assumption readily leads to the formation of specific inhibitory-to-excitatory connections through inhibitory plasticity (Vogels et al., 2011), as suggested by recent experiments (Lee et al., 2014; Xue et al., 2014; Znamenskiy et al., 2018; Najafi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to both theoretical and experimental work.

claim: The model network can generate excess population activity when novel stimuli are presented as violations of repeated stimulus sequences.
source: We demonstrate that this model network can generate excess population activity when novel stimuli are presented as violations of repeated stimulus sequences.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation results shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Plasticity of inhibitory synapses is a sufficient mechanism to explain population novelty responses and adaptive phenomena on multiple timescales.
source: Our framework identifies plasticity of inhibitory synapses as a sufficient mechanism to explain population novelty responses and adaptive phenomena on multiple timescales.
evidence: This is supported by the model results shown in Figure 4.

claim: Stimulus-specific inhibitory connectivity supports adaptation to specific stimuli (SSA).
source: In addition, stimulus-specific inhibitory connectivity supports adaptation to specific stimuli (SSA).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6.

claim: Disinhibition is a powerful regulator of the amplification of novelty responses.
source: Furthermore, we suggest disinhibition to be a powerful regulator of the amplification of novelty responses.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7.

claim: Neurons in primary sensory cortex may not signal the violation of periodicity of a sequence based on bottom-up input, but rather adapt to the distribution of presented stimuli.
source: Most intriguing, we hypothesize that neurons in primary sensory cortex may not signal the violation of periodicity of a sequence based on bottom-up input, but rather adapt to the distribution of presented stimuli.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the model results shown in Figure 3D,E.

claim: The model network consists of 4000 excitatory and 1000 inhibitory neurons.
source: The model consists of 4000 excitatory exponential integrate-and-fire (EIF) neurons and 1000 inhibitory leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neurons (Table 1).
evidence: This is a description of the model architecture.

claim: Excitatory-to-excitatory synapses were plastic based on the triplet spike-timing-dependent plasticity (eSTDP) rule.
source: Excitatory-to-excitatory (E-to-E) synapses were plastic based on the triplet spike-timing-dependent plasticity (eSTDP) rule (Sjöström et al., 2001; Pfister and Gerstner, 2006; Gjorgjieva et al., 2011; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the plasticity rule used in the model, supported by citations and shown in a figure.

claim: The triplet STDP rule enabled the formation of strong bidirectional connections among similarly selective neurons.
source: The triplet STDP rule enabled the formation of strong bidirectional connections among similarly selective neurons (Gjorgjieva et al., 2011; Montangie et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on triplet STDP.

claim: Plasticity of connections from inhibitory to excitatory neurons was based on an inhibitory STDP (iSTDP) rule measured experimentally.
source: Plasticity of connections from inhibitory to excitatory neurons was based on an inhibitory STDP (iSTDP) rule measured experimentally (D'amour and Froemke, 2015), and shown to stabilize excitatory firing rate dynamics in recurrent networks (Vogels et al., 2011; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental and theoretical work, and shown in a figure.

claim: The model only included long-term plasticity and did not explicitly model additional adaptation mechanisms.
source: In contrast to other frameworks which have found short-term plasticity as key for capturing adaptation phenomena, we only included long-term plasticity and did not explicitly model additional adaptation mechanisms.
evidence: This describes a key difference between this model and previous models.

claim: Starting from an initially randomly connected network, presenting tuned input led to the emergence of excitatory assemblies.
source: Starting from an initially randomly connected network, presenting tuned input led to the emergence of excitatory assemblies, which are strongly connected, functionally related subsets of excitatory neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, left).
evidence: This is demonstrated in the model simulations shown in the figure.

claim: Tuned input led to the stimulus-specific potentiation of inhibitory-to-excitatory connections.
source: Furthermore, tuned input also led to the stimulus-specific potentiation of inhibitory-to-excitatory connections (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E, left).
evidence: This is demonstrated in the model simulations shown in the figure.

claim: The pretraining phase imprinted structure in the network prior to the actual stimulation paradigm as a model of the activity-dependent refinement of structured connectivity during early postnatal development.
source: This pretraining phase imprinted structure in the network prior to the actual stimulation paradigm as a model of the activity-dependent refinement of structured connectivity during early postnatal development (Thompson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental work on developmental refinement.

claim: The model network generates a novelty response when presenting a novel stimulus by increasing the excitatory population firing rate at the time of stimulus presentation.
source: Importantly, the model network generates a novelty response when presenting a novel stimulus by increasing the excitatory population firing rate at the time of stimulus presentation (Näätänen et al., 2007).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1B and supported by citation to experimental literature.

claim: Novelty and onset responses were observed after as few as four sequence repetitions.
source: Novelty and onset responses were observed after as few as four sequence repetitions (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 2A.

claim: After more than 15 sequence repetitions, the averaged excitatory population activity reached a clear baseline activity level.
source: After more than 15 sequence repetitions, the averaged excitatory population activity reached a clear baseline activity level (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 2A.

claim: The novelty response amplitude increased with the number of sequence repetitions before saturating for a high number of sequence repeats.
source: The novelty response amplitude, measured by the population rate of the novelty peak minus the baseline population rate, increased with the number of sequence repetitions before saturating for a high number of sequence repeats (Figure 2B, black dots).
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 2B.

claim: The decay of the onset response depends on the number of stimuli in a sequence.
source: By averaging excitatory population responses across sequence blocks with equal length, we found that the decay of the onset response depends on the number of stimuli in a sequence (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 2C.

claim: There is a linear relationship between the number of stimuli in a sequence and the decay constant.
source: Upon fitting an exponentially decaying function to the activity of the onset response, we derived a linear relationship between the number of stimuli in a sequence and the decay constant (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 2D.

claim: Repeating sequence blocks dampened the onset response at sequence onset compared to the unique sequence stimulation paradigm.
source: We randomized the order of the sequence block presentation to avoid additional temporal structure beyond the stimulus composition of the sequences. Repeating sequence blocks dampened the onset response at sequence onset compared to the unique sequence stimulation paradigm (compare Figure 1B and Figure 2A,B with Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown by comparing the simulation results in different figures.

claim: Both excitatory and inhibitory populations adapt to the repeated stimuli and show a prominent novelty peak that is larger than the respective averaged onset response.
source: We found that both excitatory and inhibitory populations adapt to the repeated stimuli and show a prominent novelty peak that is larger than the respective averaged onset response (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 3B,C.

claim: Swapping the last and second-to-last stimulus, instead of presenting a novel stimulus, does not elicit a novelty response.
source: We found that swapping the last and second-to-last stimulus, instead of presenting a novel stimulus, does not elicit a novelty response (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 3D.

claim: Shuffling the stimuli within a sequence block still generates a novelty response and adaptation to the repeated stimuli, similar to the strictly periodic case.
source: Additionally, we asked whether the periodicity of the stimuli within a sequence influences the novelty response. Shuffling the stimuli within a sequence block still generates a novelty response and adaptation to the repeated stimuli, similar to the strictly periodic case (Figure 3E, compare to Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 3E.

claim: A reduction of the input drive decreases the novelty peak, revealing a monotonic dependence of the novelty response on stimulus strength.
source: Finally, we investigated if the novelty peak depends on the input firing rate of the novel stimulus. We found that a reduction of the input drive decreases the novelty peak, revealing a monotonic dependence of the novelty response on stimulus strength (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 3F.

claim: Novelty responses arise because inhibitory plasticity fails to sufficiently increase inhibitory input and to counteract the excess excitatory input into excitatory neurons upon the presentation of a novel stimulus.
source: We found that novelty responses arise because inhibitory plasticity fails to sufficiently increase inhibitory input and to counteract the excess excitatory input into excitatory neurons upon the presentation of a novel stimulus.
evidence: This is the mechanistic explanation derived from the model results.

claim: Adaptation in the network arises through increased inhibition onto highly active neurons through selective strengthening of I-to-E weights.
source: Adaptation in the network arises through increased inhibition onto highly active neurons through selective strengthening of I-to-E weights (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown schematically in Figure 4A and demonstrated in the model results.

claim: The inhibitory weights onto stimulus-specific assemblies tuned to the stimuli in a given sequence increased upon presentation of the corresponding sequence block, and decreased otherwise.
source: The inhibitory weights onto stimulus-specific assemblies tuned to the stimuli in a given sequence increased upon presentation of the corresponding sequence block, and decreased otherwise (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 4B.

claim: The population firing rate during repeated presentation of a sequence decreased (adapted) on the same timescale as the increase of the inhibitory weights related to this sequence.
source: The population firing rate during repeated presentation of a sequence decreased (adapted) on the same timescale as the increase of the inhibitory weights related to this sequence (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 4C.

claim: Adaptation occurs on multiple timescales in the model: milliseconds (inhibitory plasticity), seconds (sequence block presentation), and minutes (multiple sequence blocks).
source: Interestingly, we found that adaptation occurs on multiple timescales in our model. The fastest is the timescale of milliseconds on which inhibitory plasticity operates, the next slowest is the timescale of seconds corresponding to the presentation of a sequence block, and finally the slowest is the timescale of minutes corresponding to the presentation of the same sequence block multiple times (Figure 4D, top; also compare Figure 1B and Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results across multiple figures.

claim: The generation of novelty responses does not depend on the exact sequence structure of stimulus presentations, as long as the overall distribution of stimuli is maintained.
source: Therefore, our results suggest that the exact sequence structure of stimulus presentations is not relevant for the novelty response, as long as the overall distribution of stimuli is maintained.
evidence: This is inferred from the model results showing that shuffling stimuli does not affect novelty responses.

claim: Increasing the number of repetitions in the pretraining phase increased the height of the novelty peak, but eventually reached a plateau at 10 repetitions.
source: Specifically, increasing the number of repetitions in the pretraining phase increased the height of the novelty peak, but eventually reached a plateau at 10 repetitions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Increasing the number of stimuli decreased the height of the novelty peak.
source: Increasing the number of stimuli decreased the height of the novelty peak (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Inhibitory plasticity needs to be fast for both the generation of a novelty response and adaptation to repeated stimuli.
source: We found that inhibitory plasticity needs to be fast for both results, the generation of a novelty response (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B) and adaptation to repeated stimuli (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: An increase in the inter-repetition interval reduced the adaptation level of the excitatory population.
source: We found that an increase in the inter-repetition interval reduced the adaptation level of the excitatory population (Figure 5A,D) due to a decrease of inhibitory synaptic strength onto stimulus-specific assemblies (Figure 5B,E).
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 5.

claim: Longer inter-repetition intervals provide more time for the inhibitory weights onto stimulus-specific assemblies to decrease, hence, weakening the adaptation.
source: In summary, longer inter-repetition intervals provide more time for the inhibitory weights onto stimulus-specific assemblies to decrease, hence, weakening the adaptation.
evidence: This is the mechanistic explanation derived from the model results in Figure 5.

claim: The network with inhibitory plasticity and tuned inhibitory neurons was able to generate SSA.
source: Upon presenting stimulus A several times, the neuronal response gradually adapted to the baseline level of activity, while presenting the oddball stimulus B resulted in an increased population response (Figure 6B). Therefore, this network was able to generate SSA.
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 6B.

claim: SSA could neither be generated with adaptive neurons and static synapses, nor with inhibitory plasticity without inhibitory tuning.
source: In our model network, SSA could neither be generated with adaptive neurons and static synapses (Figure 6C, top; Materials and methods), nor with inhibitory plasticity without inhibitory tuning (Figure 6C, bottom).
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 6C.

claim: Including an adaptive current in the model neurons did not lead to adaptation of the response to a frequent stimulus since firing rates rapidly adapted during stimulus presentation and completely recovered in the inter-stimulus pause.
source: In fact, including an adaptive current in the model neurons (Brette and Gerstner, 2005) did not even lead to adaptation of the response to a frequent stimulus since firing rates rapidly adapted during stimulus presentation and completely recovered in the inter-stimulus pause (Figure 6C, top).
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 6C, top.

claim: During the presentation of stimulus A, stimulus-specific inhibitory weights corresponding to stimulus A increased their strength, while stimulus-specific inhibitory weights corresponding to stimulus B remained low.
source: During the presentation of stimulus A, stimulus-specific inhibitory weights corresponding to stimulus A (average weights from inhibitory neurons tuned to stimulus A onto excitatory neurons tuned to stimulus A, see Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, right) increased their strength, while stimulus-specific inhibitory weights corresponding to stimulus B remained low (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 6D.

claim: After a 9 s pause, the response remained adapted.
source: After a 9 s pause, the response remained adapted (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Only after more than 200 s the response fully recovered.
source: Only after more than 200 s the response fully recovered (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Disinhibition amplified the novelty response.
source: When repeating the SSA experiment (Figure 6) and applying such a disinhibitory signal (inhibition of the inhibitory population) at the time of the novel stimulus B, our model network amplified the novelty response (Figure 7B, shaded green, also compare to Figure 6B, top).
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 7B.

claim: Disinhibition increased the density of the network response which corresponds to the number of active excitatory neurons.
source: Disinhibition also increased the density of the network response which corresponds to the number of active excitatory neurons (Figure 7C, left).
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 7C.

claim: Disinhibition increased the fraction of active excitatory neurons.
source: Indeed, disinhibition increased the fraction of active excitatory neurons, which we defined as the fraction of neurons that spike at least once in a 100 ms window during the presentation of a stimulus (Figure 7C, right).
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 7C.

claim: Without a disinhibitory signal, the fraction of active neurons for a novel stimulus in the model was qualitatively similar as for repeated stimuli and therefore there was no dense novelty response.
source: Without a disinhibitory signal, the fraction of active neurons for a novel stimulus in our model was qualitatively similar as for repeated stimuli and therefore there was no dense novelty response (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Disinhibition can flexibly amplify the novelty peak and increase the density of novelty responses.
source: In sum, we found that by controlling the total disinhibitory strength (Materials and methods), disinhibition can flexibly amplify the novelty peak (Figure 7D) and increase the density of novelty responses (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 7D,E.

claim: Inhibitory plasticity is the key mechanism behind the generation of adapted and novelty responses in the model.
source: In summary, we identified the plasticity of connections from inhibitory to excitatory neurons belonging to a stimulus-specific assembly as the key mechanism in our framework for the generation of novelty responses and for the resulting adaptation of the network response to repeated stimuli.
evidence: This is the main conclusion from the model results.

claim: Experimental studies have characterized spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) of synapses from inhibitory onto excitatory neurons.
source: Many experimental studies have characterized spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) of synapses from inhibitory onto excitatory neurons (Holmgren and Zilberter, 2001; Woodin et al., 2003; Haas et al., 2006; Maffei et al., 2006; Wang and Maffei, 2014; D'amour and Froemke, 2015; Field et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: In theoretical studies, network models usually include inhibitory plasticity to dynamically stabilize recurrent network dynamics.
source: In theoretical studies, network models usually include inhibitory plasticity to dynamically stabilize recurrent network dynamics (Vogels et al., 2011; Litwin-Kumar and Doiron, 2014; Zenke et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical studies.

claim: Daily passive sound exposure has been found to lead to an upregulation of the activity of inhibitory neurons.
source: In the context of habituation, daily passive sound exposure has been found to lead to an upregulation of the activity of inhibitory neurons (Kato et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to an experimental study.

claim: Increased activity to a deviant stimulus in the MMN is diminished when inhibitory neurons are suppressed.
source: Furthermore, increased activity to a deviant stimulus in the MMN is diminished when inhibitory neurons are suppressed (Hamm and Yuste, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to an experimental study.

claim: Blocking NMDA receptors can disrupt the MMN.
source: However, there exists some discrepancy in how exactly NMDA receptors are involved in SSA (Ross and Hamm, 2020), since blocking NMDA receptors can disrupt the MMN (Tikhonravov et al., 2008; Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: If the background activity between stimulus presentations in the model is very low, recovery from adaptation will only happen on a very slow timescale.
source: Therefore, if the background activity between stimulus presentations in our model is very low, recovery from adaptation will only happen on a very slow timescale (as in Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is explained based on the model mechanism and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: If the activity between stimulus presentations is higher, the adapted stimulus can recover faster.
source: However, if the activity between stimulus presentations is higher (either because of a higher background firing rate or because of evoked activity from other sources, for example other stimuli), the adapted stimulus can recover faster (as in Figure 5).
evidence: This is explained based on the model mechanism and shown in Figure 5.

claim: The model can capture the reduced adaptation for longer inter-stimulus intervals as found in experiments when background activity in the inter-stimulus interval is elevated.
source: Therefore, we conclude that our model can capture the reduced adaptation for longer inter-stimulus intervals as found in experiments (Ulanovsky et al., 2004; Cohen-Kashi Malina et al., 2013) when background activity in the inter-stimulus interval is elevated.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the model results and comparison to experimental findings.

claim: Excitatory short-term depression, usually of thalamocortical synapses, is the most widely hypothesized mechanism to underlie adaptive phenomena in cortex.
source: Excitatory short-term depression, usually of thalamocortical synapses, is the most widely hypothesized mechanism to underlie adaptive phenomena in cortex (Nelken, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Short-term plasticity can be different at the synapses from PV and SOM interneurons onto pyramidal neurons, and can generate diverse temporal responses in pyramidal neurons in the auditory cortex.
source: Experimental work has shown that short-term plasticity can be different at the synapses from PV and SOM interneurons onto pyramidal neurons, and can generate diverse temporal responses (facilitated, depressed and stable responses) in pyramidal neurons in the auditory cortex (Seay et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to an experimental study.

claim: Short-term plasticity can capture the differences in responses to periodic versus random presentation of repeated stimuli in a sequence.
source: Short-term plasticity can also capture the differences in responses to periodic versus random presentation of repeated stimuli in a sequence (Yaron et al., 2012; Chait, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental and theoretical studies.

claim: Short-term plasticity has been suggested to explain forward masking in the auditory cortex.
source: Finally, short-term plasticity has been suggested to explain a prominent phenomenon in the auditory cortex, named 'forward masking' (Brosch and Schreiner, 1997), in which a preceding masker stimulus influences the response to a following stimulus (Phillips et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Experimental studies find adaptation timescales from hundreds of milliseconds to tens of seconds.
source: Experimental studies find adaptation timescales from hundreds of milliseconds to tens of seconds (Ulanovsky et al., 2004; Lundstrom et al., 2010; Homann et al., 2017; Latimer et al., 2019), and in the case of habituation even multiple days (Haak et al., 2014; Ramaswami, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The timescales of short-term plasticity can range from milliseconds to minutes.
source: At the same time, the timescales of short-term plasticity can range from milliseconds to minutes (Zucker and Regehr, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Inhibitory plasticity can readily lead to adaptation on multiple timescales without the need for any additional assumptions.
source: Our work shows that inhibitory plasticity can readily lead to adaptation on multiple timescales without the need for any additional assumptions (Figure 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated in the model results shown in Figure 4.

claim: It is unclear whether inhibitory plasticity can act sufficiently fast to explain adaptation phenomena on the timescale of seconds.
source: However, it is unclear whether inhibitory plasticity can act sufficiently fast to explain adaptation phenomena on the timescale of seconds, as in our model (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: Most computational models of recurrent networks with plastic connections rely on fast inhibitory plasticity to stabilize excitatory rate dynamics.
source: Most computational models of recurrent networks with plastic connections rely on fast inhibitory plasticity to stabilize excitatory rate dynamics (Sprekeler, 2017; Zenke et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical studies.

claim: Decreasing the learning rate of inhibitory plasticity five-fold eliminates the adaptation to repeated stimuli and the novelty response in the model.
source: Decreasing the learning rate of inhibitory plasticity five-fold eliminates the adaptation to repeated stimuli and the novelty response in our model (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: During the induction of inhibitory plasticity, inhibitory postsynaptic currents increase significantly immediately after the induction of plasticity.
source: Experimentally, during the induction of inhibitory plasticity, spikes are paired for several minutes and it takes several tens of minutes to reach a new stable baseline of inhibitory synaptic strength (D'amour and Froemke, 2015; Field et al., 2020). Nonetheless, inhibitory postsynaptic currents increase significantly immediately after the induction of plasticity (see e.g. D'amour and Froemke, 2015; Field et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Changes of inhibitory synaptic strength already occur while the plasticity induction protocol is still ongoing.
source: This suggests that changes of inhibitory synaptic strength already occur while the plasticity induction protocol is still ongoing.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations cited.

claim: Inhibitory long-term plasticity is a suitable candidate to explain the generation of novelty responses and adaptive phenomena over multiple timescales.
source: Hence, we propose that inhibitory long-term plasticity is a suitable, though not the only, candidate to explain the generation of novelty responses and adaptive phenomena over multiple timescales.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the model results and experimental evidence.

claim: Varying the pretraining duration and the number of pretraining stimuli did not qualitatively change the novelty response and its properties.
source: Varying the pretraining duration and the number of pretraining stimuli did not qualitatively change the novelty response and its properties (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Presenting different stimuli in the stimulation phase compared to the pretraining phase preserved the adaptation to repeated stimuli and the generation of a novelty response.
source: In addition, presenting different stimuli in the stimulation phase compared to the pretraining phase (Materials and methods) to mimic the scenario of randomly oriented Gabor patches in Homann et al., 2017, preserved the adaptation to repeated stimuli and the generation of a novelty response (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Slowing normalization down did not affect the generation of adapted and novelty responses.
source: However, slowing normalization down did not affect the generation of adapted and novelty responses (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Slow inhibitory plasticity failed to homeostatically stabilize firing rates in the network.
source: Slow inhibitory plasticity failed to homeostatically stabilize firing rates in the network. Hence, the network no longer showed an adapted response to repeated stimuli and novelty responses became indiscernible from noise (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The model observed an active amplification of the novelty response upon including a top-down disinhibitory signal.
source: Upon including a top-down disinhibitory signal in our model network, we observed: (1) an active amplification of the novelty response (Figure 7B)
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 7B.

claim: The model observed a dense novelty response upon including a top-down disinhibitory signal.
source: (2) a dense novelty response (Figure 7C), similar to experimental findings (Homann et al., 2017) (without a disinhibitory signal, the novelty response was not dense, see Figure 1—figure supplement 4)
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 7C and compared to experimental findings.

claim: The model observed a flexible manipulation of neuronal responses through a change in the disinhibitory strength.
source: (3) a flexible manipulation of neuronal responses through a change in the disinhibitory strength (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 7D,E.

claim: Inhibitory neurons in primary sensory areas can be shaped by diverse neuromodulatory signals, which allow for subtype-specific targeting of inhibitory neurons.
source: First, inhibitory neurons in primary sensory areas can be shaped by diverse neuromodulatory signals, which allow for subtype-specific targeting of inhibitory neurons (Froemke, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Higher order feedback onto layer 1 inhibitory cells could mediate the behavioral relevance of the adapted stimuli through a disinhibitory pathway.
source: Second, higher order feedback onto layer 1 inhibitory cells could mediate the behavioral relevance of the adapted stimuli through a disinhibitory pathway (Letzkus et al., 2011; Wang and Yang, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The active amplification of novelty responses generated by the model is consistent with some experimental data.
source: The active amplification of novelty responses generated by our model is consistent with some experimental data (Taaseh et al., 2011; Hershenhoren et al., 2014; Hamm and Yuste, 2016; Harms et al., 2016), but see also Vinken et al., 2017.
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Giving a behavioral meaning to a sound through fear conditioning has been shown to modify SSA.
source: Giving a behavioral meaning to a sound through fear conditioning has been shown to modify SSA (Yaron et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to an experimental study.

claim: Contrast adaptation has been shown to reverse when visual stimuli become behaviorally relevant.
source: Similarly, contrast adaptation has been shown to reverse when visual stimuli become behaviorally relevant (Keller et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to an experimental study.

claim: As soon as a stimulus becomes behaviorally relevant, inhibitory neurons decrease their response and therefore disinhibit adapted excitatory neurons.
source: Other studies have also shown that as soon as a stimulus becomes behaviorally relevant, inhibitory neurons decrease their response and therefore disinhibit adapted excitatory neurons (Kato et al., 2015; Makino and Komiyama, 2015; Hattori et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Attention might lead to activation of the disinhibitory pathway, allowing for a change in the novelty response compared to the unattended case.
source: Attention might lead to activation of the disinhibitory pathway, allowing for a change in the novelty response compared to the unattended case, as suggested in MMN studies (Sussman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to an experimental study.

claim: In habituation, the idea that a change in context can assign significance to a stimulus and therefore block habituation, leading to 'dehabituation', is widely accepted.
source: Especially in habituation, the idea that a change in context can assign significance to a stimulus and therefore block habituation, leading to 'dehabituation', is widely accepted (Ramaswami, 2014; Barron et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Disinhibition is a flexible mechanism to control several aspects of novelty responses, including the density of the response.
source: Hence, we suggest that disinhibition is a flexible mechanism to control several aspects of novelty responses, including the density of the response, which might be computationally important in signaling change detection to downstream areas (Homann et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the model results and supported by citation to experimental work.

claim: The model is an attractor network that differs from classic attractor models where inhibition is considered unspecific.
source: In theoretical terms, our model is an attractor network. It differs from classic attractor models where inhibition is considered unspecific (like a 'blanket') (Amit and Brunel, 1997).
evidence: This is a characterization of the model and comparison to previous models.

claim: Inhibitory assemblies can improve the robustness of attractor dynamics.
source: These studies have argued that inhibitory assemblies can improve the robustness of attractor dynamics (Rost et al., 2018) and keep a local balance of excitation and inhibition (Rostami et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical studies.

claim: Specific inhibitory connections readily follow from a tuned inhibitory population.
source: We showed that specific inhibitory connections readily follow from a tuned inhibitory population (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in the model results.

claim: Adaptation is linked to a stimulus-specific excitatory/inhibitory (E/I) balance.
source: Our results suggest that adaptation is linked to a stimulus-specific excitatory/inhibitory (E/I) balance.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the model results.

claim: Presenting a novel stimulus leads to a short-term disruption of the E/I balance, triggering inhibitory plasticity, which aims to restore the E/I balance.
source: Presenting a novel stimulus leads to a short-term disruption of the E/I balance, triggering inhibitory plasticity, which aims to restore the E/I balance (Figure 4; Vogels et al., 2011; D'amour and Froemke, 2015; Field et al., 2020).
evidence: This is shown in the model results and supported by citations.

claim: Disinhibition, which effectively disrupts the E/I balance, allows for flexible control of adapted and novelty responses.
source: Disinhibition, which effectively disrupts the E/I balance, allows for flexible control of adapted and novelty responses (Figure 7).
evidence: This is shown in the model results in Figure 7.

claim: Disinhibition is a gating mechanism for learning and plasticity.
source: This links to the notion of disinhibition as a gating mechanism for learning and plasticity (Froemke et al., 2007; Letzkus et al., 2011; Kuhlman et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The detection of unexpected (or novel) events follows from the lack of selective adaptation to those events.
source: We showed that one of these roles, the detection of unexpected (or novel) events, follows from the lack of selective adaptation to those events.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the model results.

claim: According to predictive coding, the overall goal of our brain is to minimize the prediction error.
source: According to predictive coding, the overall goal of our brain is to minimize the prediction error, that is the difference between the internal prediction and the sensory input (Rao and Ballard, 1999; Clark, 2013; Friston, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work on predictive coding.

claim: Most predictive coding schemes hypothesize the existence of prediction error units and prediction population units.
source: Most predictive coding schemes hypothesize the existence of two populations of neurons. First, prediction error units that signal a mismatch between the internal model prediction and the incoming sensory stimuli. And second, a prediction population unit that reflects what the respective layer 'knows about the world' (Rao and Ballard, 1999; Clark, 2013; Spratling, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work on predictive coding.

claim: The model suggests that primary sensory areas allow for bottom-up detection of stimulus changes without the need for an explicit population of error neurons or an internal model of the world.
source: Our model suggests that primary sensory areas allow for bottom-up detection of stimulus changes without the need for an explicit population of error neurons or an internal model of the world.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the model results.

claim: One could interpret the state of all inhibitory synaptic weights as an implicit internal model of the recent frequency of various events in the environment.
source: However, one could also interpret the state of all inhibitory synaptic weights as an implicit internal model of the recent frequency of various events in the environment.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the model results.

claim: Inhibitory plasticity might serve as an essential mechanism underlying many adaptive phenomena.
source: First, the most general implication from our study is that inhibitory plasticity might serve as an essential mechanism underlying many adaptive phenomena.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the model results.

claim: Inhibitory plasticity allows for adaptation on multiple timescales, ranging from the adaptation to sequence blocks on the timescale of seconds to slower adaptation on the timescale of minutes.
source: Our work suggests that inhibitory plasticity allows for adaptation on multiple timescales, ranging from the adaptation to sequence blocks on the timescale of seconds to slower adaptation on the timescale of minutes, corresponding to repeating multiple sequence blocks (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is shown in the model results in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Both excitatory and inhibitory neuron populations show adaptive behavior and novelty responses.
source: A second prediction follows from the finding that both excitatory and inhibitory neuron populations show adaptive behavior and novelty responses (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is shown in the model results in Figure 3B,C.

claim: Adaptation of inhibitory neurons on the single-cell level has already been verified experimentally.
source: Adaptation of inhibitory neurons on the single-cell level has already been verified experimentally (Chen et al., 2015; Natan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: A violation of the sequence order does not lead to a novelty response.
source: Third, we further predict that a violation of the sequence order does not lead to a novelty response. Therefore, the novelty response should not be interpreted as signaling a violation of the exact sequence structure (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is shown in the model results in Figure 3D,E.

claim: Previous work has found a reduction in the response to repeated stimuli if the stimuli are presented periodically, rather than randomly, in a sequence.
source: However, previous work has found a reduction in the response to repeated stimuli if the stimuli are presented periodically, rather than randomly, in a sequence (Yaron et al., 2012) (but see Mehra et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The height of the novelty peak in the population average depends on the input drive, where decreasing the input strength decreases the novelty response.
source: Fourth, the height of the novelty peak in the population average depends on the input drive, where decreasing the input strength decreases the novelty response (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is shown in the model results in Figure 3F.

claim: The main types of inhibitory neurons, parvalbumin-positive (PV), somatostatin-positive (SOM), and vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) expressing neurons, differ in their connectivity and their hypothesized functional roles.
source: The main types of inhibitory neurons, parvalbumin-positive (PV), somatostatin-positive (SOM), and vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) expressing neurons, differ in their connectivity and their hypothesized functional roles (Tremblay et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Studies of the influence of inhibitory neurons on adaptation have shown that different interneuron types have unique contributions to adaptation.
source: Studies of the influence of inhibitory neurons on adaptation have shown that different interneuron types have unique contributions to adaptation (Kato et al., 2015; Natan et al., 2015; Hamm and Yuste, 2016; Natan et al., 2017; Garrett et al., 2020; Heintz et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The model has proposed a mechanistic model for the emergence of adapted and novelty responses based on inhibitory plasticity, and the regulation of this novelty response by top-down signals.
source: In sum, we have proposed a mechanistic model for the emergence of adapted and novelty responses based on inhibitory plasticity, and the regulation of this novelty response by top-down signals.
evidence: This is a summary of the main contributions of the study.

claim: The findings could be further relevant for disorders like schizophrenia where adapted responses are perturbed.
source: Our findings offer insight into the flexible and adaptive responses of animals in constantly changing environments, and could be further relevant for disorders like schizophrenia where adapted responses are perturbed (Hamm et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to an experimental study.
